name: Hermann Oppenheim

summary.text: Hermann Oppenheim was a Prussian-born banker with houses in Paris and Alexandria whose firm, Oppenheim, Neveu & Co., arranged several of Khedive Ismail's loans. U.S. diplomatic correspondence of 1874 records the firm taking half of a £32 million Egyptian loan in 1873 at 75 and the balance in 1874 after public subscription largely failed.

facts.claim: U.S. diplomatic correspondence reports that Oppenheim, Neveu & Co. took £16 million of the 1873 Egyptian loan at 75 with an option on the rest after public subscription largely failed, and took the balance of the £32 million loan in 1874.

facts.claim: A 1969 Soviet history describes Oppenheim as Prussian-born, treated as a British subject, owning banks in Paris and Alexandria, and as having arranged most of the loans of Said and Ismail; the same work states that of an 1864 loan of £5.7 million the Egyptian Treasury received about £4.86 million.

openQuestions: Site claim tested: 'arranged several of Ismail's loans' is supported by the FRUS correspondence and Lutsky. The page's totals (£68 million nominal, £46 million received, 1862-73) were not found in any source returned; an 1870s Egyptian government summary quoted in a library scan gives about £26.9 million of proceeds for the decade to September 1873, which does not match either figure.
Lutsky's history is a Soviet-era work with a strong interpretive frame; treat its characterisations with caution.
